Gold and silver miners are back in focus after weaker bullion prices pressured margins and analysts cut earnings estimates, putting Agnico Eagle Mines (NYSE:AEM) under the spotlight as it engages investors at recent mining conferences.

Agnico Eagle Mines has been pulled lower with the sector, with the share price down 11.97% over the past 30 days and 21.84% over 90 days, even after a recent 3.03% 1-day rebound to US$161.20 and a 6.54% 7-day share price return that hints at stabilising sentiment. Total shareholder return still shows a long-run payoff, with a decline of 6.77% over 1 year set against very large gains over 3 and 5 years that reflect how strongly long-term holders have previously been rewarded as views on growth potential and risk have shifted.

Bears see a gold miner exposed to weaker bullion and tighter margins, while bulls point to Agnico Eagle Mines’ pullback and long record in the sector. Which story fits the current valuation work best?

Most Popular Narrative: 99.9% Undervalued

The narrative fair value of $123,914 for Agnico Eagle Mines sits far above the last close at $161.20, setting up an extremely aggressive upside case that goes well beyond recent share price weakness.

According to lenny67, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the key swing factor is how Agnico Eagle Mines might respond to operational challenges at the Canadian Malartic complex and the potential role of a neighboring micro-cap in that equation.

Because the Barnat open pit was entering its final years of production (scheduled to wind down by early 2029), stabilizing a collapsed rock mass might be an outright financial loss. Shifting millions of tonnes of waste rock just to access the bottom of an expiring pit is an engineering nightmare. Instead, Agnico is masking the gap by chewing through low-grade surface stockpiles, a strategy that will heavily compress profit margins when full data hits the wire during their Q2 earnings call on July 29, 2026.

Readers weighing that argument may want to contrast it with the current share price, recent returns and forecasts that point to flat revenue growth of around 0.4% per year and an expected earnings decline of 0.9% per year over the next three years, then decide how much weight to place on such an optimistic scenario.

Still, this scenario depends on successful execution at Canadian Malartic and assumes that any third party deal terms or timing align with Agnico Eagle Mines shareholders’ interests.

While the narrative fair value for Agnico Eagle Mines points to an extreme upside case, the market’s own yardstick tells a calmer story. A P/E of 13.2x is only slightly above the US Metals and Mining group on 13.1x, and below the peer average of 15.8x.
